findings.claim_text: A PIC (Programmable Interface Controller) is a popular family of microcontroller chip.
findings.issue: The lesson expands PIC as 'Programmable Interface Controller'. The correct original expansion is 'Peripheral Interface Controller' (the name given by General Instrument when the PIC1640 was developed). Microchip Technology, who produce the PIC family today, do not use PIC as an acronym at all. 'Programmable Interface Controller' is a fabricated expansion that appears nowhere in authoritative documentation and could cause students to write incorrect answers in the exam.
findings.correct_version: Change to: 'A PIC (Peripheral Interface Controller) is a popular family of microcontroller chip.' Alternatively, since Microchip Technology no longer treats PIC as an acronym, the safest phrasing is: 'A PIC microcontroller (PIC was originally short for Peripheral Interface Controller) is a popular family of microcontroller chip.'

findings.claim_text: Dyson's cyclonic vacuum technology is a well-known example of technology push. James Dyson developed the cyclonic separation principle — using centrifugal force to spin dust out of an airstream without a bag — and then built a product around it.
findings.issue: The description of technology push is accurate and the Dyson claim is broadly correct. No specific dates or prototype counts mentioned in this lesson — claim is general and not fact-checkable to the level of requiring a correction.

findings.claim_text: Efficiency of commercially available panels typically ranges from around 15–22% for silicon cells.
findings.issue: This range is accurate for standard/mid-range silicon PV panels. Premium monocrystalline panels can now reach 22–24% but the 15–22% range is a defensible and commonly cited figure for commercially available panels in 2025/26. No error.

findings.claim_text: Polymorph … becomes soft and mouldable when placed in warm water (approximately 62°C)
findings.issue: Accurate. Polymorph (polycaprolactone) has a softening point of approximately 60–62°C. Confirmed by multiple manufacturer and materials datasheets.

findings.claim_text: the wings and fuselage sections of aircraft such as the A350 are predominantly CFRP
findings.issue: The claim about the A350 being predominantly CFRP is accurate (A350 = ~52% CFRP including wing skins and fuselage). However, lesson 19 separately attributes substantial CFRP use to the A380 ('composite materials replaced heavier aluminium in key structural sections'), which is partially accurate but potentially misleading — the A380 uses only ~16–25% composites overall, with GLARE (aluminium-glass laminate) in the upper fuselage, not predominantly CFRP. The lesson 5 claim itself (attributing predominantly-CFRP to the A350) is correct and causes no error. The A380 framing in lesson 19 is the weaker claim (assessed there).

findings.claim_text: Kevlar is a synthetic para-aramid fibre developed by DuPont. It has exceptionally high tensile strength — around five times stronger than steel by weight
findings.issue: Both claims are accurate. Kevlar was developed by Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont in 1965 and is widely quoted as approximately 5× stronger than steel by weight (tensile strength ~3,000 MPa at density 1.44 g/cm³ vs steel ~400–500 MPa at density ~7.85 g/cm³). The lesson does not name Kwolek as inventor — omission acceptable at GCSE level.

findings.claim_text: professional packages such as AutoCAD or SolidWorks can cost thousands of pounds per seat per year
findings.issue: Accurate general claim. No specific price given that could be checked against a standard. No errors.

findings.claim_text: A0 has an area of exactly 1 m². The aspect ratio remains constant at 1:√2 (approximately 1:1.414). ISO 216 standard.
findings.issue: Both claims are accurate. A0 is defined as 841 × 1189 mm (area ≈ 1 m²) with aspect ratio 1:√2. ISO 216 is the correct standard number. Copy paper at 80 gsm and ~100 microns is also accurate.

findings.claim_text: Balsa — extremely low density (as low as 100–200 kg/m³), making it the lightest commercial timber.
findings.issue: The density range given (100–200 kg/m³) is accurate for commercial-grade balsa (typical range 100–250 kg/m³; some sources cite 120–160 kg/m³ for commercially preferred grades). Balsa is confirmed as the lightest commercial timber. No error.

findings.claim_text: Cast iron contains 2–4% carbon. Mild steel (low-carbon steel) contains 0.1–0.3% carbon. Tensile strength approximately 400–500 MPa. Aluminium has a density of approximately 2.7 g/cm³ — about one third the density of steel. Copper is an excellent electrical conductor (second only to silver). Brass — copper (roughly 65%) and zinc (roughly 35%). Bronze — copper and tin (historically around 88% copper, 12% tin).
findings.issue: All key figures verified: cast iron 2–4% C correct; mild steel 0.1–0.3% C with tensile strength 400–500 MPa correct (some sources cite up to 550 MPa but 400–500 is the standard quoted range); aluminium density 2.7 g/cm³ correct (steel ~7.85 g/cm³, ratio ~1:3 accurate); copper second to silver in electrical conductivity correct; brass 65% Cu / 35% Zn correct (this is cartridge brass / high brass, the most commonly cited ratio); bronze ~88% Cu / 12% Sn is a well-established modern standard composition. No errors.

findings.claim_text: HDPE has a melting point of approximately 130°C. Polypropylene (~160–170°C). Polypropylene density approximately 0.9 g/cm³. Formica is a trade name for MF-laminated board. Araldite is a consumer epoxy adhesive.
findings.issue: All verified: HDPE melting point 125–140°C (130°C is a standard quoted figure, accurate); PP melting point 160–170°C correct; PP density 0.9–0.91 g/cm³ correct (floats in water accurate); Formica uses melamine-formaldehyde for the surface layer (core uses phenol-formaldehyde, but 'MF-laminated board' is acceptable and standard GCSE shorthand); Araldite is correctly identified as an epoxy adhesive (brand of Huntsman). No errors.

findings.claim_text: Silk — from the cocoon of the silkworm (Bombyx mori). The silkworm spins a continuous filament up to 900 metres long. Cashmere — typically 150–200 g per goat per year.
findings.issue: Silk filament length: sources vary widely (300m–1,500m depending on strain and conditions); 'up to 900 metres' is within the cited range and not misleading. Cashmere yield: 150–200g is confirmed by multiple specialist sources. No errors.

findings.lesson_title: Investigating the Work of Designers and Companies
findings.claim_text: After reportedly over 5,000 prototype iterations across five years, the G-Force cyclonic vacuum cleaner was launched in 1983 in Japan before reaching the UK market in 1993 as the DC01.
findings.issue: The G-Force was designed in 1983 but was not manufactured and sold in Japan until 1986 (produced by APEX Inc. for the Japanese market in March 1986, priced at the equivalent of US$2,000). Saying it was 'launched in 1983 in Japan' conflates the design year with the market launch year by three years. Additionally, the first Dyson-branded UK vacuum was the DA 001 (January 1993), which was shortly replaced by the DC01. Referring to the UK launch as 'the DC01' is a simplification but broadly acceptable at GCSE level. The '1983 in Japan' date is the error requiring correction.
findings.correct_version: Change to: '…the G-Force cyclonic vacuum cleaner was designed in 1983 and launched in Japan in 1986, before Dyson brought the technology to the UK market in 1993 as the DC01.'

findings.lesson_title: Investigating the Work of Designers and Companies
findings.claim_text: Under Jony Ive as Chief Design Officer, Apple developed a design philosophy built on simplicity, material quality, and the removal of unnecessary elements. Products like the iMac G3 (1998), the iPod (2001), and the iPhone (2007) succeeded…
findings.issue: The Apple product dates are correct (iMac G3: shipped August 1998; iPod: October 2001; iPhone: June 2007). However, Jony Ive was not 'Chief Design Officer' during the creation of these products. He held the title of Senior Vice President of Industrial Design from the late 1990s until May 2015, when he was promoted to the newly created Chief Design Officer role. The iMac G3, iPod and first iPhone were all designed under his SVP title, not CDO. Calling him 'Chief Design Officer' throughout implies a title that postdates the iMac G3 by 17 years.
findings.correct_version: Change to: 'Under Jony Ive, initially as Senior Vice President of Industrial Design and later as Chief Design Officer (from 2015), Apple developed a design philosophy built on simplicity…'

findings.lesson_title: Investigating the Work of Designers and Companies
findings.claim_text: His most studied product is the Juicy Salif citrus squeezer (1990, manufactured by Alessi).
findings.issue: The year is ambiguous. The Juicy Salif design dates from 1988 (sketched on a napkin during a restaurant visit), but it was first produced and sold in 1990. MoMA catalogs it as '1988'. Alessi and Wikipedia both cite 1990 as the production year. For a GCSE context, '1990' is defensible as the production/launch year, so this is a low-severity issue rather than an error. The description of it as cast aluminium with three legs is accurate. The claim that 'juice splashes rather than being channelled' is accurate — Starck himself confirmed the squeezer was 'not meant to squeeze lemons'.
findings.correct_version: Optional clarification: '(designed 1988, first manufactured 1990, by Alessi)' — but 1990 as a standalone year is acceptable for GCSE.

findings.lesson_title: Investigating the Work of Designers and Companies
findings.claim_text: Dyson's hand dryer removes water by forcing air across the hands at 430 mph
findings.issue: The Dyson Airblade V (HU02) specification confirms 430 mph airspeed at the apertures. Earlier models operated at ~400 mph and the newer 9kJ model operates at 388 mph, but 430 mph is accurate for the most commonly referenced Airblade V model. No error.

findings.lesson_title: Investigating the Work of Designers and Companies
findings.claim_text: Matthew Williamson has collaborated with companies including Debenhams and Pucci
findings.issue: Both accurate. Williamson collaborated with Debenhams from 2001 (one of the first high-street designer collaborations) and served as Creative Director at Pucci from 2006 to 2008. No error.

findings.claim_text: Products for children must be tested against requirements such as choking-hazard rules (no component smaller than 45 mm in any direction for products intended for children under 3).
findings.issue: This is factually wrong. The EU Toy Safety Directive (2009/48/EC) and EN 71-1 use a small parts test cylinder measuring 57.1 mm tall by 31.7 mm diameter. A 'small part' is any component that fits entirely inside this cylinder (i.e., it is too small — roughly equivalent to a part that could fit in a child's throat). The lesson inverts the logic and gives a wrong dimension (45 mm). No toy safety standard defines a minimum safe size as '45 mm in any direction'. A student using this figure in an exam answer would be writing incorrect information about a named regulation.
findings.correct_version: Change to: 'Products for children must be tested against the small parts requirements of EN 71-1 (under the EU Toy Safety Directive). The small parts test uses a cylinder 57.1 mm tall and 31.7 mm in diameter — any component that fits entirely inside this cylinder is classified as a choking hazard and must not be present in toys intended for children under 3.'
